etymology: From biblical (according to Scripture) and marriage (Old French mariage, the wedded estate); the covenant union God ordained at creation.
biblical_def: Biblical marriage is the lifelong covenant union of one man and one woman before God, ordained by the Creator at the beginning, before the fall and before any nation or church, as the first and most fundamental of human institutions. God made them male and female, and said, “Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.” The Lord Jesus reaffirmed this creation pattern against the loose divorce practice of His day, returning to Genesis: “What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.” Marriage is thus a divine institution, not a human invention to be redefined at will; its terms are fixed by the God who made it. It is the union of two sexes, male and female, the only category of legitimate sexual union; it is monogamous, one man and one woman; it is a covenant, entered by vow before God and binding for life; and it is ordered, with the husband as head and the wife as helper, reflecting the order of creation. Marriage also bears a sacred typology: it images the union of Christ and His church, the husband’s sacrificial headship picturing Christ’s love and the wife’s glad submission picturing the church’s. The dictionary holds biblical marriage as the creational and unchangeable standard, the foundation of the family and of society, given by God for companionship, the bearing and rearing of godly children, and the picture of the gospel.
webster_summary: The lifelong covenant union of one man and one woman before God, ordained at creation, the only legitimate sexual union, ordered as a picture of Christ and His church.
webster_full: BIBLICAL MARRIAGE, the covenant union of one man and one woman before God.

“A man shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
Monogamous, lifelong, and ordered, with the husband as head and the wife as helper.
A picture of the union of Christ and His church.

corruption_summary: Marriage is severed from its creation design and redefined by the will of man to include unions Scripture forbids.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption is the redefinition of marriage by the will of man—the claim that marriage is a social construct to be reshaped at will, so that two men or two women may be “married,” or that the sexes themselves may be denied. Scripture forecloses this: God made them male and female and joined the man to his wife, and the Lord Jesus anchored marriage in that unchangeable creation order. What God has defined, no court, culture, or church may redefine; the union of two persons of the same sex is no marriage but a violation of the creation ordinance, and the denial of the two sexes is a corruption of Genesis itself.

A second corruption is the cheapening of marriage even where its form is kept—cohabitation that refuses the covenant, easy divorce that breaks it, and a contractual view that treats it as a temporary arrangement of mutual convenience. The dictionary holds marriage as God made it: a lifelong covenant of one man and one woman, ordered and exclusive, honorable in all, and the appointed picture of Christ and His church. To redefine it is to attack the gospel it images and the society it founds; the church’s task is not to follow the age but to hold and honor the creation ordinance.

etymology: From marriage and vow (Latin votum, a solemn promise made before God); the binding promise that constitutes the marriage covenant.
biblical_def: The marriage vow is the solemn promise, made before God and witnesses, by which a man and a woman bind themselves to each other in the covenant of marriage for life. Marriage is a covenant, and a covenant is constituted by vows; the prophet Malachi calls the wife “the wife of thy covenant,” and rebukes the men who dealt treacherously against the wives to whom they had pledged themselves. A vow is no light thing in Scripture: “When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed.” The marriage vow is taken in the presence of God, who is witness between the man and the wife, and who holds both to their word. By it each gives himself to the other exclusively and permanently—to have and to hold, for better or worse, in sickness and in health, forsaking all others, till death parts them. The vow is therefore the ground of marital faithfulness: the bond is not the feeling of love, which may ebb, but the pledged word, which stands; and to break the vow by adultery, desertion, or treacherous divorce is to sin against the spouse, against the covenant, and against God who witnessed it. The dictionary holds the marriage vow as the binding heart of marriage: a sacred promise that creates a permanent bond, to be kept in the fear of God through every season, because the God who heard it requires its payment.
webster_summary: The solemn promise, made before God and witnesses, by which a man and woman bind themselves in the marriage covenant for life—the pledged word that constitutes and secures the bond.
webster_full: MARRIAGE VOW, the solemn promise constituting the marriage covenant.
Made before God, who is witness between the man and the wife.
Malachi calls the wife “the wife of thy covenant.”
A vow is binding: “pay that which thou hast vowed.”
The ground of faithfulness is the pledged word, not the changeable feeling.

corruption_summary: The marriage vow is treated as a sentiment to be revised, so that the bond is thought to last only while the feeling does.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that marriage rests on a vow, not a mood. The age treats the bond as lasting only so long as love is felt, so that when affection cools the vow is held void. Scripture binds the conscience to the pledged word: the LORD was witness, the wife is the wife of the covenant, and the vow must be paid. Faithfulness is the keeping of a promise through every season, not the persistence of an emotion.

A second corruption hollows the vow even where it is spoken—reciting “till death do us part” while privately reserving the option of divorce, so that the most solemn promise a man makes is uttered with crossed fingers. The dictionary holds the vow in its full weight: it is made before God, who hears and requires it, and to break it by treachery is to sin against the spouse and against the God who witnessed it. The marriage vow is sacred, binding, and lifelong, and the fear of God is the surest guard of the marriage bed.
roots_summary: The phrase names the binding promise that constitutes marriage, made before God who witnesses and requires it.

etymology: From wifely (befitting a wife) and submission (Greek hupotassō, to arrange under, to yield to order); the wife’s ordered yielding to her husband’s headship.
biblical_def: Wifely submission is the wife’s glad and reverent yielding to the loving headship of her own husband, commanded in Scripture as her part in the creational order of marriage. “Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as unto the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church.” This submission is grounded not in any inferiority of the wife—husband and wife are equally image-bearers of God and equally heirs of the grace of life—but in the order God established at creation, for Adam was first formed, then Eve. It is voluntary, rendered to her own husband and not to men generally; it is dignified, the response of an equal who freely honors God’s appointed order, not the cringing of a slave; it is limited, never requiring obedience to sin, for the wife’s first allegiance is to the Lord; and it is reciprocal in setting, for it is answered by the husband’s costly, sacrificial love. The wife’s submission images the church’s submission to Christ, as the husband’s love images Christ’s love for the church. Peter adds that even an unbelieving husband may be won without the word by the chaste behavior of his wife and the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price. The dictionary holds wifely submission as a creation ordinance and a Christian virtue, neither tyranny on the husband’s part nor servility on the wife’s, but the beautiful ordering of marriage after the pattern of Christ and His church.
webster_summary: The wife’s glad, reverent yielding to her own husband’s loving headship—grounded in the creation order, not inferiority—imaging the church’s submission to Christ.
webster_full: WIFELY SUBMISSION, the wife’s ordered yielding to her husband’s headship.
“Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as unto the Lord.”
Grounded in the creation order, not in any inferiority of the wife.
Voluntary, dignified, and limited—never requiring obedience to sin.
Images the church’s submission to Christ; answered by the husband’s sacrificial love.

corruption_summary: Submission is condemned as patriarchal oppression and erased by egalitarianism, or distorted into servility by domineering men.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption is egalitarianism, which reads the command to submit as a relic of patriarchy to be discarded, and insists that any ordered headship and submission demeans the wife. But Scripture grounds submission not in inferiority—the wife is equally an image-bearer and joint-heir—but in the creation order, Adam first formed, then Eve, an order older than the fall and reaffirmed by the apostles. To call God’s creational design oppression is to charge the Creator with injustice; the dictionary names the egalitarian framing as the corruption and holds the apostolic command.

The opposite corruption is the abuse of the doctrine by domineering men who twist headship into tyranny and submission into servility—demanding obedience to sin, ruling by harshness, and forgetting that the husband is commanded to love his wife as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for it. The dictionary rejects both distortions. Wifely submission is voluntary, dignified, and bounded by obedience to God; it is answered by sacrificial love; and rightly ordered, it is no burden but a beauty, the marriage reflecting the union of Christ and His church.

etymology: From creation and order (an arrangement, a structure of authority); the abiding structure God built into the world at creation.
biblical_def: The creation order is the abiding structure that God built into the world at the beginning, before the fall, by which He arranged human life—the two sexes, marriage, headship and submission, work and rest, and the family—according to His wisdom. Because these things were established at creation, they are not the changeable customs of a passing culture but the fixed design of the Creator, binding on all peoples in all ages. The apostle Paul repeatedly grounds his teaching not in local custom but in creation: the man is the head of the woman because Adam was first formed, then Eve; the man is the image and glory of God, and the woman the glory of the man, for the man is not of the woman, but the woman of the man, neither was the man created for the woman, but the woman for the man. So too the Lord Jesus grounds marriage and its permanence in the creation pattern, “from the beginning,” God made them male and female. The creation order is good, for God pronounced His finished work very good; it is not the product of the fall, though the fall has marred its working and bred the abuse of authority and the rebellion against it. The dictionary holds the creation order as the unchangeable foundation for the doctrines of the two sexes, marriage, and complementarian headship: what God ordered at creation is binding still, and the modern attempt to dismiss it as mere ancient culture is itself the rebellion against the Creator that Scripture names.
webster_summary: The abiding structure God built into the world at creation—the two sexes, marriage, headship, work and rest—fixed by the Creator and binding in all ages, not changeable custom.
webster_full: CREATION ORDER, the abiding structure God built into the world at the beginning.
Arranges the two sexes, marriage, headship, work and rest, and the family.
Established before the fall, fixed by the Creator, binding on all peoples.
Paul grounds his teaching in creation: “Adam was first formed, then Eve.”
Good, for God pronounced His finished work very good.

corruption_summary: The creation order is dismissed as mere ancient culture, so that its fixed design for sex, marriage, and headship is treated as negotiable.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption dismisses the creation order as the bound custom of a patriarchal ancient world, no longer binding on an enlightened age—so that the two sexes, marriage, and headship are recast as social constructions open to revision. But Paul and the Lord Jesus ground these very things not in custom but in creation, “from the beginning,” and what the Creator built into the world at the first is binding still. To wave away the creation order as outdated culture is to set the creature’s wisdom above the Creator’s, the very rebellion of the fall.

The dictionary holds the creation order as fixed and good. It is not a product of sin—it was pronounced very good before the fall—though sin has marred its working, breeding both the tyrannical abuse of authority and the rebellious rejection of it. The remedy is not to abolish the order but to redeem its working in Christ, so that headship is exercised in sacrificial love and submission rendered in glad reverence. The two sexes are God’s good design, marriage His good institution, and the ordering of the home His good arrangement; the age may deny them, but it cannot unmake what God ordered at creation.
roots_summary: The phrase names the fixed structure God built into the world at creation, binding for sex, marriage, and headship.

etymology: From male and eldership (the office of elder); the New Testament restriction of the ruling and teaching office to qualified men.
biblical_def: Male eldership is the New Testament restriction of the office of elder—the ruling and teaching office of the church—to qualified men. The apostle Paul, grounding his instruction in the creation order rather than in passing custom, writes: “Let the woman learn in silence with all subjection. But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence. For Adam was first formed, then Eve.” The qualifications for the office assume a man: the elder must be “the husband of one wife,” one that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection. This restriction is not a judgment on the worth, gifts, or spiritual standing of women, who are equally image-bearers, equally redeemed, and equally heirs of glory, and who labor indispensably in the church in countless ways; it is rather the maintaining of the order God established at creation, the same order that governs the home. The eldership is one office, also called pastor, bishop, and overseer, and the plurality of elders is the New Testament pattern; in all its forms the ruling and authoritative teaching of the gathered church belongs to qualified men. The dictionary holds male eldership as the clear apostolic teaching, grounded in creation and therefore binding in every age and culture: the church honors and employs the gifts of women fully, yet reserves the office of elder to men, not as a concession to ancient society but in obedience to the abiding command of God.
webster_summary: The New Testament restriction of the ruling and teaching office of elder to qualified men, grounded in the creation order—not a judgment on the worth or gifts of women.

corruption_summary: Male eldership is overthrown by egalitarianism, which dismisses Paul’s command as mere culture and ordains women to the ruling office.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption is egalitarianism, which sets aside the apostolic restriction by claiming it was merely Paul’s accommodation to ancient society, binding then but not now. But Paul does not appeal to local custom; he grounds his instruction in creation—“Adam was first formed, then Eve”—and what is grounded in creation is binding in every age. The ordination of women to the eldership, however well-intentioned, overturns the order God established and the command His apostle gave; the dictionary names the egalitarian reading as the corruption and holds the plain text.

The doctrine must be guarded against caricature. Male eldership is not the silencing or demeaning of women, who are equally image-bearers and joint-heirs, who prophesied in both Testaments, who taught children and younger women, who carried letters and instructed in private, and whose labors the church cannot do without. It restricts one thing only: the office of ruling and authoritative public teaching elder, reserved to qualified men. The dictionary holds this as obedience, not chauvinism—the church gladly honoring and employing the gifts of women while keeping the office as God appointed it.

etymology: From covenant and household (the family and all under one roof); the family as a unit of covenant blessing and responsibility.
biblical_def: The covenant household is the family considered as a unit under the covenant of God—the believing head, his wife, his children, and all his house—within which the worship, instruction, and discipline of the Lord are carried on, and upon which the promises and obligations of the covenant rest. Scripture again and again deals with God’s people not merely as isolated individuals but as households. God establishes His covenant with Abraham and his seed after him; Joshua resolves, “as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD”; the Philippian jailer believed and was baptized, he and all his straightway. The household is the primary place of religious nurture: the father is charged to bring up his children in the nurture and admonition of the Lord, to teach them the words of God diligently when he sits in his house and walks by the way, and to command his household after him to keep the way of the LORD. This does not teach that grace runs automatically in the bloodline—every child must come to personal faith—but it does mean that God ordinarily works through covenant homes, that the children of believers are set in a place of privilege under the means of grace, and that parents bear a solemn charge for the souls of their children. The dictionary holds the covenant household as a recovery against the radical individualism of the age: God saves persons, but He ordinarily gathers them in families, and the believing home, ordered under its head and devoted to family worship and instruction, is a chief instrument of His covenant purpose from generation to generation.
webster_summary: The family as a unit under God’s covenant—the believing head, wife, children, and house—the primary place of worship, instruction, and discipline, set under the covenant’s promises and duties.

corruption_summary: The covenant household is dissolved by individualism, which treats faith as a purely private matter unrelated to family and generations.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God ordinarily deals with His people in households and across generations, not merely as isolated individuals. The radical individualism of the age treats faith as a wholly private affair, severs the child from the covenant nurture of the home, and forgets the solemn charge laid upon parents for their children’s souls. Scripture sets family worship, daily instruction, and household devotion at the center of God’s ordinary working.

The doctrine must be guarded from the opposite error of presumption—the notion that grace runs automatically in the bloodline, so that a child born to believers is saved by birth without personal faith. The dictionary holds the balance: every soul must come to Christ personally, yet the children of believers are set in a place of high privilege under the means of grace, and God delights to work through covenant homes. The believing household, ordered under its head and devoted to the worship and instruction of the Lord, is a chief instrument of His covenant purpose from generation to generation.

etymology: From no-fault (requiring no proof of wrongdoing) and divorce (Latin divortium, a turning apart); the modern legal dissolution of marriage at the will of either party.
biblical_def: No-fault divorce is the modern legal arrangement by which a marriage may be dissolved at the will of either spouse, without any proof of wrongdoing—a revolution in law and custom that made the breaking of the marriage covenant as easy as the breaking of any contract of convenience. Measured against Scripture, no-fault divorce is a grievous corruption of God’s law of marriage. The Lord Jesus, appealing to creation, declared marriage a one-flesh union that God Himself joins and that man must not put asunder, and taught that Moses suffered divorce only for the hardness of men’s hearts, but from the beginning it was not so. Scripture permits the sundering of marriage in only narrow and grievous cases—the sexual unfaithfulness of a spouse, and the desertion of a believer by an unbeliever—and even then as a sorrowful concession, not a casual option. No-fault divorce sweeps all this away, treating the most solemn covenant a man can make as terminable at whim, and the LORD declares that He hates the treacherous putting away of a wife. The dictionary names no-fault divorce as a corruption of the marriage covenant and a chief engine of the breakdown of the family: it teaches that vows are provisional, that covenants bind only while convenient, and that the one-flesh union God forbade man to sunder may be dissolved at pleasure. The church’s calling is to honor the permanence of marriage, to hold the narrow biblical grounds, and to bear faithful witness against the easy divorce the age has normalized.
webster_summary: The modern legal dissolution of marriage at either spouse’s will without proof of wrongdoing—a corruption of God’s law of marriage, which permits sundering only on narrow, grievous grounds.
webster_full: NO-FAULT DIVORCE, the dissolution of marriage at either spouse’s will without proof of fault.

corruption_summary: No-fault divorce is itself the corruption—the treating of the marriage covenant as a terminable contract of convenience.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. No-fault divorce is itself the corruption to be named. It enshrines in law the lie that the marriage covenant binds only while it pleases, that the most solemn vow a man makes may be revoked at will, and that the one-flesh union God forbade man to sunder may be dissolved without cause. The Lord Jesus traced easy divorce to the hardness of the human heart and recalled men to the creation pattern; no-fault divorce is the legal triumph of that hardness.

The dictionary holds the biblical doctrine against the age. Marriage is a covenant that God Himself joins, and He hates its treacherous breaking. Scripture permits the sundering of marriage only on narrow and grievous grounds—the sexual betrayal of a spouse, and the desertion of a believer by an unbeliever—and even then with sorrow, as a concession to sin, not a casual right. Against the easy divorce the age has normalized, the church must hold the permanence of marriage, exercise patient pastoral care for the wounded, and bear plain witness that the vows men make before God are binding for life.

etymology: From mixed and faith; a marriage between a believer and an unbeliever, also called an unequal yoke.
biblical_def: A mixed-faith marriage is a marriage between a believer and an unbeliever—a child of God joined to one outside the covenant—which Scripture forbids the believer to enter, though it instructs those already in such a marriage how to walk. The command is plain: the believer is to marry “only in the Lord,” and not to be “unequally yoked together with unbelievers,” for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness, and what communion hath light with darkness. The Old Testament warned Israel repeatedly against intermarriage with the idolatrous nations, not on grounds of race but of religion, because such unions turned the heart after other gods, as even Solomon’s wives turned away his heart. The danger is spiritual: the marriage that should be a partnership in the faith and a covenant home for godly seed becomes instead a house divided at its deepest point, with the believer pulled toward compromise and the children torn between two masters. Yet Scripture does not command the breaking of a mixed marriage already contracted; if an unbelieving spouse is content to dwell with the believer, let the believer not depart, for the unbelieving spouse is sanctified by the believing, and the believer may, by a holy walk, be the means of the other’s salvation. The dictionary holds the doctrine in both its parts: the believer is forbidden to enter a mixed-faith marriage and ought to marry only in the Lord; but the one already so married is called not to abandon the spouse, but to adorn the gospel at home and pray and hope for the other’s conversion.
webster_summary: A marriage between a believer and an unbeliever—the unequal yoke Scripture forbids the believer to enter, though it bids those already so married to remain and seek the spouse’s salvation.
webster_full: MIXED-FAITH MARRIAGE, a marriage between a believer and an unbeliever.
Forbidden to enter: marry “only in the Lord,” “be ye not unequally yoked.”
The danger is spiritual—the heart turned after other gods, as Solomon’s was.
Yet the believer already so married is not to depart from a willing spouse.
The unbelieving spouse is sanctified by the believing; salvation may follow a holy walk.
scriptures: Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?
The wife is bound by the law as long as her husband liveth; but if her husband be dead, she is at liberty to be married to whom she will; only in the Lord.
And the woman which hath an husband that believeth not, and if he be pleased to dwell with her, let her not leave him.
For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods: and his heart was not perfect with the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father.
corruption_summary: The command to marry only in the Lord is dismissed as narrow, and the spiritual danger of the unequal yoke is denied.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the command to marry “only in the Lord” and not to be unequally yoked. An age that prizes romantic feeling above spiritual oneness treats this command as narrow and unloving, and counsels believers to marry where the heart inclines regardless of faith. Scripture warns otherwise: the closest of unions, when divided at its deepest point, breeds compromise in the believer and confusion in the children, as the history of Israel and of Solomon shows.

The doctrine must be guarded from a harsh misuse. Scripture forbids entering a mixed marriage but does not command breaking one already contracted; the believer married to a willing unbeliever is to remain, to walk holily, and to seek the spouse’s salvation, for the unbelieving spouse is sanctified by the believing and may be won. The dictionary holds both: a solemn warning to the unmarried to marry only in the Lord, and a tender counsel to the already-yoked believer to be faithful at home and hopeful in prayer, that the partner of the body might become a partner in the faith.
roots_summary: The phrase names the believer-unbeliever marriage—the unequal yoke forbidden to enter, yet to be honored where it already exists.
roots_lines: Greek heterozugeo — to be unequally yoked, joined with a different kind.
“Only in the Lord” — the limit set upon the believer’s freedom to marry.
The Old Testament warnings against intermarriage rest on religion, not race.
Greek hagiazo — to sanctify; the unbelieving spouse “sanctified” by the believing.
Solomon’s foreign wives “turned away his heart after other gods.”
usage: Mixed-faith marriage is taught as the unequal yoke believers are forbidden to enter.
“Only in the Lord” guides the unmarried believer’s choice of a spouse.
Paul’s counsel guides the believer already married to a willing unbeliever.

etymology: From Latin paterfamilias (the father and head of a household) and authority; the God-given headship of the father over his household.
biblical_def: Paterfamilial authority is the God-given headship of the father over his household—his wife, his children, and all under his roof—by which he leads, provides, protects, instructs, and governs the home in the fear of the Lord. The man is appointed head of the wife as Christ is head of the church, and father of his children, charged to rule his own house well and to have his children in subjection with all gravity, for if a man know not how to rule his own house, how shall he take care of the church of God? This authority is not absolute, for the father is himself under authority—under Christ his Head, accountable to God for every soul in his charge—and it is not tyrannical, for fathers are commanded not to provoke their children to wrath, but to bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord, and husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church. The father’s headship is therefore a stewardship of loving service, exercised for the good of those under him, after the pattern of Christ who came not to be ministered unto but to minister. It carries solemn duty: family worship, the instruction of the children in the Scriptures, the discipline of the home, and the provision and protection of the household. The dictionary holds paterfamilial authority as a creation ordinance and a Christian charge, the foundation of the ordered home and a chief bulwark of a godly society—an authority to be neither abdicated by passive or absent fathers, nor abused by harsh and domineering ones, but exercised in humble, sacrificial, accountable headship under Christ.
webster_summary: The God-given headship of the father over his household—to lead, provide, protect, instruct, and govern in the fear of the Lord—a stewardship of sacrificial service under Christ, neither abdicated nor abused.
webster_full: PATERFAMILIAL AUTHORITY, the father’s God-given headship over his household.
He leads, provides, protects, instructs, and governs the home in the fear of the Lord.
Charged to rule his own house well and bring up his children in the Lord.
Not absolute—he is under Christ, accountable to God for every soul in his charge.
Not tyrannical—fathers must not provoke their children, but love and nurture them.
scriptures: One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity;
Eph 6:4
And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
For I know him, that he will command his children and his household after him, and they shall keep the way of the LORD, to do justice and judgment;
But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
corruption_summary: Fatherly headship is either denounced as oppressive patriarchy and erased, or abused into harsh domination divorced from sacrificial love.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption on one side denounces all fatherly headship as oppressive patriarchy and seeks to erase it—leaving homes without godly male leadership, fathers passive or absent, and children ungoverned. But Scripture grounds the father’s headship in God’s appointment, not in any tyranny to be abolished; the answer to bad fathers is not no fathers but good ones, exercising loving, sacrificial, accountable authority after the pattern of Christ. The dictionary names the wholesale denunciation of fatherly authority as a corruption that has wounded countless homes.

The opposite corruption is the abuse of the doctrine—the harsh, domineering father who turns headship into petty tyranny, provokes his children to wrath, rules by fear, and forgets that he is himself under Christ and accountable for every soul in his house. The dictionary rejects both the abdication and the abuse. Paterfamilial authority is a stewardship of loving service: the father leads as one who must give account, provides and protects as Christ provides for His church, and governs not to gratify himself but for the good of those entrusted to him. Such fathers are a chief blessing of a godly home and a bulwark of a stable society.
roots_summary: The phrase names the father’s headship of his household—a sacrificial, accountable authority under Christ, the foundation of the ordered home.
roots_lines: Latin paterfamilias — the father and head of a household.
Greek proistēmi — to rule, preside, lead; “ruleth well his own house.”
The father is under authority—under Christ, accountable to God.
Bounded by love: “provoke not your children to wrath.”
Exercised in family worship, instruction, discipline, provision, and protection.
usage: Paterfamilial authority grounds the father’s leadership of family worship and instruction.
It is held between the abdication of passive fathers and the abuse of domineering ones.
Its accountability under Christ is stressed against both denial and tyranny.

etymology: From Latin caelibatus, the unmarried state; the condition of remaining unmarried, especially for the sake of undistracted service to God.
biblical_def: Celibacy is the state of remaining unmarried, which Scripture honors as a lawful and, for some, a gifted calling for the sake of undistracted service to God—while firmly rejecting the imposition of compulsory celibacy as a requirement for office or a higher class of holiness. The Lord Jesus spoke of those who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven’s sake, and bade him receive it who is able. The apostle Paul, himself unmarried, commended the single state for its freedom from the cares that attend marriage, that the unmarried might care for the things of the Lord without distraction and attend upon Him without hindrance; yet he expressly named singleness a gift not given to all, taught that it is better to marry than to burn, and honored marriage as honorable in all. Celibacy in Scripture is therefore neither commanded nor exalted above marriage, but left free: a good calling for those gifted and willing, undertaken for service, not as a meritorious work. The dictionary holds this biblical balance against the Roman corruption that forbids marriage to its priests and elevates the celibate religious life as a counsel of perfection. Paul named the forbidding of marriage among the doctrines of devils that mark a falling away from the faith; what God has left free, the church may not bind. The dictionary commends celibacy where it is a genuine gift for the kingdom’s service, honors the marriage God ordained for the rest, and rejects every system that makes the single state a law, a merit, or a higher holiness.
webster_summary: The unmarried state, honored in Scripture as a lawful and gifted calling for undistracted service to God—but never commanded, never meritorious, and not to be imposed as compulsory.
webster_full: CELIBACY, the state of remaining unmarried.
Honored for some as a gifted calling for undistracted service to God.
Christ’s “eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven’s sake”; Paul commends the single state.
A gift not given to all; “it is better to marry than to burn.”
Neither commanded nor exalted above marriage; the forbidding of marriage is condemned.
scriptures: For I would that all men were even as I myself. But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that.
But I would have you without carefulness. He that is unmarried careth for the things that belong to the Lord, how he may please the Lord:

For there are some eunuchs, which were so born from their mother’s womb: and there are some eunuchs, which were made eunuchs of men: and there be eunuchs, which have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven’s sake. He that is able to receive it, let him receive it.
Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth.
corruption_summary: Celibacy is corrupted into a compulsory law for clergy and a higher class of holiness, against the freedom Scripture leaves.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning corruption is the Roman imposition of compulsory celibacy upon its priests and the elevation of the celibate religious life as a counsel of perfection—a higher holiness than the married estate. Scripture leaves the single state free, a gift for some and a calling for service, never a law or a merit. Paul names the forbidding of marriage among the “doctrines of devils” that mark a departure from the faith, and the qualifications for elder assume a married man, “the husband of one wife.” What God has left free, the church may not bind, and the mandatory celibacy of the clergy has borne bitter fruit through the centuries.

The dictionary holds the biblical balance. Celibacy is honorable where it is a genuine gift, undertaken willingly for undistracted devotion to the Lord, and the church should esteem the single believer who serves Christ without the cares of marriage. But it is not superior to marriage, which God ordained at creation and pronounced good; it is not meritorious, earning no special favor; and it is not to be imposed. Against both the Roman exaltation of compulsory celibacy and any modern disdain for the single life, the dictionary keeps the apostolic freedom: marriage is honorable in all, singleness is a good gift for some, and each is to serve God in the calling he is given.
roots_summary: The word names the unmarried state, honored as a gift for service but never commanded, meritorious, or imposed.
roots_lines: Latin caelibatus — the unmarried state, from caelebs, unmarried.
Christ’s “eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven’s sake” (Matthew 19:12).
Greek charisma — gift; singleness a “proper gift of God” for some.
Paul’s counsel: the unmarried “careth for the things... of the Lord.”
“Forbidding to marry” named among the “doctrines of devils.”
usage: Celibacy is honored as a gifted calling for undistracted service to the Lord.
Paul’s teaching is cited that it is a gift not given to all and not above marriage.
It is set against the Roman imposition of compulsory clerical celibacy.
